chapter_theme: True giving is giving to those who have nothing, and everything else is a kind of loan. The chapter ranks giving above reward, above ascetic endurance and even above life itself, and it argues from the giver's own joy and safety as well as from virtue.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the definition of ஈகை (221), the excellence of giving (222-227), and the fault of not giving (228-230).

221.reading: Giving something to those who have nothing is what giving is; all the rest has the nature of a measured loan.
221.nuance: குறியெதிர்ப்பு is a technical word: taking a stated measure and returning that same measure, as Parimelazhagar glosses it. All gifts among equals are thus reclassified, however generous they feel.

222.reading: Even if it were called a good path, taking is bad; even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
222.nuance: The verse cuts the value of giving loose from its reward by a hypothetical. How strong that hypothetical is, is exactly what the commentators disagree about.

positions.position: Both 'even ifs' are purely hypothetical: no one actually says such things, and heaven isn't in doubt.
positions.quote: 'எனினும்' என்பது இரு வழியும் அங்ஙனம் கூறுவார் இன்மை விளக்கி நின்றது.

positions.position: Giving won't obtain any higher world, and the giving life is best regardless.
positions.quote: கொடை வழங்குவதால் மேலுலகம் என்று சொல்லப்படுவது கிட்டிவிடப் போவதில்லை;

223.reading: Not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing', and giving, are found only in one of good family.
223.nuance: Parimelazhagar lists several rival interpretations, including giving before the asker has to speak, and giving so that he need not go on to ask anyone else.

positions.position: These are two virtues: not begging oneself, and not refusing those who beg.
positions.quote: யான் வறியன் என்று இரப்பான் சொல்லும் இளிவரவைத் தான் பிறர்கண் சொல்லாமையும்

positions.position: It is one act: giving without telling the suppliant 'I have nothing'.
positions.quote: இரந்து வந்தார்க்கு இல னென்னாகின்ற துன்பத்தைக் கூறாது ஈதலும்

positions.position: It means giving without showing the distress of one's own poverty.
positions.quote: தமக்குள்ள வறுமைத் துன்பத்தைக் காட்டிக்கொள்ளாமல் பிறருக்கு ஈவது

224.reading: Being begged from is itself painful, until one sees the glad face of the one who begged.
224.nuance: A candid observation: being asked is uncomfortable even for the generous. Parimelazhagar attributes this to fear of not being able to give all that is sought.

positions.position: இரக்கப்படுதல் is being the one asked, and resolving to give.
It is feeling pity (இரக்கம்) for the supplicant, a different root.

225.reading: The strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that ranks behind the strength of those who remove hunger.
225.nuance: The verse says only ஆற்றுவார், those with strength. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both understand ascetics, which makes this a direct ranking of the giver over the renunciant. Parimelazhagar's reason is that the ascetic hungers and can't relieve others.

226.reading: Removing the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where a person who has come into wealth should store it.
226.nuance: அழிபசி is hunger that destroys: Parimelazhagar says all goods, Manakkudavar says a person's qualities. The financial image is made pointed by Parimelazhagar: the wealth comes back to help the giver. He supplies 'for virtue's sake' himself, so the verse is plainer about the bank than he is.

227.reading: The evil disease called hunger is unlikely to touch one who is habituated to sharing his food.
227.nuance: Manakkudavar reads this as a reply to the miser's fear that giving will lead to hunger. Understood that way, the verse is a piece of argument rather than a promise. மரீஇ makes the claim about habit, not about any one gift.

positions.position: It answers the fear that giving will reduce wealth and bring on hunger.

228.reading: Do those hard-eyed people who hoard what they have and then lose it not know the joy of giving and gladdening?
228.nuance: The appeal is to pleasure, not to duty: the hoarder has simply missed out. 'Keep and lose' in one word, வைத்திழக்கும், makes the loss seem part of keeping. Parimelazhagar's own wording suggests the joy belongs to those with அருள், so this reaches forward to chapter 25.

229.reading: Eating alone to fill up one's own store is surely more bitter than begging.
229.nuance: Parimelazhagar's comparison: begging has only a moment's humiliation and no lasting poverty, while the solitary eater has both. The verse takes the worst thing most people can think of and names something worse.

positions.position: நிரப்பிய refers to filling a fixed hoard target, so the fault is accumulation.
positions.quote: ஒரோ எண்களைக்குறித்து அத்துணை ஈட்டுதும் என ஈட்டத்தையே மேற்கொண்டு இவறக் கூட்டுதல்.

positions.position: It refers to the food one has obtained, and தமியர் to eating out of everyone's sight.

230.reading: Nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach.
230.nuance: The chapter's last ranking sets giving above life. Parimelazhagar's reason is that it frees one from a bodily burden no use to anyone. This is hyperbole about value, not advice to die, and Kalaignar softens it to a comparison of pains.

links.note: On Manakkudavar's reading of 212, wealth is for helping those who deserve it. 221 says that true giving goes to those who lack. The worthy recipient and the needy recipient are different tests, and these chapters leave both standing.

222 calls taking bad even if it were a path to heaven. 1051 permits begging from the right people and puts any blame on the one who refuses. The chapters on giving and begging judge the same act from different standpoints.

229 names something worse than begging; 1066 says that nothing disgraces the tongue more than begging, even for a cow's water. Their standards differ: the misery of a life against the shame of an act.
225 places enduring hunger below removing it. 261 defines austerity as endurance plus not harming living things, so the austerity that 225 ranks low is not the fuller ideal of chapter 27.
228 asks whether hoarders know the joy they forfeit. 1001 gives the outcome: he dies without eating what he amassed, and nothing remains to be done with it.

source_issues: 222: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
